data.title: Pearl Launches Second Opinion 3D, Bringing FDA-Cleared CBCT Imaging AI to General Dentists for the First Time
data.ai_summary: Pearl launched Second Opinion 3D, making its FDA-cleared CBCT imaging AI available to general dentists in the US and Canada. The product adds embedded specialist radiology-report requests and automatic conversion of CBCT findings into insurance claim-ready documentation. AI-powered pathology detection is available in Canada and pending approval in additional markets.
data.full_text:
Key Takeaways:

Pearl has launched Second Opinion 3D, making its FDA-cleared 3D imaging AI available to general dentists in the US and Canada.

The commercial release of the FDA cleared technology adds two workflow features built specifically for general dentists: an embedded specialist radiology-report request, and automatic conversion of CBCT findings into insurance claim-ready documentation.

Built for chairside use rather than specialist image review, Second Opinion 3D is designed to help general dentists interpret CBCT scans and walk patients through what the AI finds in real time.



LOS ANGELES, Sept. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Pearl today launched Second Opinion 3D, putting its FDA-cleared 3D imaging AI into general dentists' hands as a commercial product for the first time. General practices are adopting CBCT faster than the software built to support them: most viewers on the market were designed for specialist image review, not for a general dentist working through a normal patient appointment. Second Opinion 3D is Pearl's answer: a CBCT tool built around how general practices actually work, and integrated into the same Second Opinion interface providers already use for 2D imaging.

The launch builds on the FDA 510(k) clearance Pearl received last year , when it became the first dental AI company cleared by the FDA for both 2D and 3D radiologic image analysis. That clearance covered the underlying AI, which automatically identifies structures such as the mandible, maxillary complex, nasal space, airway, inferior alveolar nerve canal, and individual teeth in CBCT scans. Today's launch turns that clearance into a product: alongside general availability, Second Opinion 3D now lets providers request a report from a board-certified oral and maxillofacial radiologist without leaving the interface, and automatically converts 3D findings into insurance claim-ready documentation, two steps that previously required separate portals and manual staff work.

“General dentists have invested in CBCT for years, but reading these scans well has traditionally required specialist-level training most practices don’t have. Second Opinion 3D helps every dentist do more with CBCT. That matters beyond the tooth being treated: CBCT is one of the more exciting imaging modalities we have because of what it can reveal about a patient's health beyond their mouth. By making CBCT more accessible and useful for dentists, we’re advancing a technology that has a role to play in bridging the gap between dental medicine and systemic health."

— Ophir Tanz, CEO and Founder, Pearl

"What I really wanted was something that would scan every slice, flag anything worth a second look, and take me straight to it. That's exactly what it does. It's caught things I would've missed just focusing on the one area I came in to check. And when I'm sitting with a patient, I can isolate exactly what I'm looking at and show them, instead of trying to explain a blob on a screen. That changes how confident patients feel about the treatment plan we land on."

— Dr. Todd Yerondopoulos, Enamel Creations, Pleasanton, CA

What does this mean for general dentists?

CBCT has moved from a specialist tool into everyday use in general practice, but the software built to support it hasn't kept pace, and the workflow around it hasn't either. Getting a specialist's opinion on a scan typically means exporting files and going through a separate referral process, and turning a 3D finding into something a payor will accept for a claim is manual work that falls to practice staff. Both add friction to a workflow that's already asking general dentists to interpret imaging outside their usual training.







Second Opinion 3D is Pearl's answer to that gap, now available as a full product rather than just a cleared technology. The AI automatically segments key anatomy and color-codes each for easy visualization, allowing users to remove or highlight specific anatomical structures. It presents anatomical structures in an interactive viewer with 3D rendering, zoom and rotation, opacity controls, length measurement. Second Opinion 3D also supports radiology-report requests and claim-ready documentation, and the ability to easily turn CBCT scans into claim-ready 2D images features mean providers no longer have to leave the software or hand work off to staff to get a second opinion or bill for what they found.

How does this compare to existing CBCT viewers?

Most CBCT software was designed for technical image review, engineered for radiologists and specialists first, with general dentists and practice workflow as an afterthought. Second Opinion 3D is built the other way around. Where a traditional workflow requires downloading a scan and uploading it to a separate radiology portal, Second Opinion 3D keeps that request inside the same software. Where turning a 3D finding into claim documentation has meant manual rework by staff, Second Opinion 3D generates it automatically. And where most viewers assume the person reading the scan is a specialist, Second Opinion 3D is also built for the general dentist and the chairside conversation.







What happens next?

Second Opinion 3D also includes AI-powered pathology detection, covering findings such as TMD, carotid artery calcifications, impactions, periapical radiolucency, and sinus radiopacities. These capabilities are currently available in Canada and pending regulatory approval in additional markets.

For multi-location practices and DSOs, Second Opinion 3D can standardize how CBCT is reviewed, documented, and communicated across locations and providers.



About Pearl

Pearl is a dental AI company committed to enhancing how patient care is delivered. Founded in 2019 by a team with decades of experience developing successful, enterprise-grade computer vision solutions, Pearl introduced the first-ever FDA-cleared AI capable of reading and instantly identifying diseases in dental x-rays. With regulatory clearance in 120 countries, Pearl's AI assists dentists in making precise clinical decisions and effectively communicating with patients, thereby transforming the dental care experience worldwide. As dentistry's global AI leader, Pearl is committed to the ongoing innovation of robust, accessible AI tools that improve patient health outcomes and build greater trust in dental medicine. To request a demo, please visit hellopearl.com/demo .

data.ai_summary: Dental AI company Pearl released the Pearl Oral Health Index, a large-scale radiographic census analyzing millions of dental visits in the US to reveal significantly higher levels of untreated caries than previously reported by government surveys. The analysis found that untreated caries is at least 4.5 times more common and the average number of decayed teeth per patient is 8.7 times higher than estimates from the CDC's National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. The report also highlighted significant geographical inequalities in access to care, noting higher extraction rates in 'dental deserts' and comparing treatment patterns between the US and UK healthcare systems.

# Pearl AI reveals hidden oral health crisis

[Home](/)/[Dental news](/news/)

News

[News](/news)
[Pearl AI reveals hidden oral health crisis](https://us.dental-tribune.com/news/pearl-ai-reveals-hidden-oral-health-crisis/)

share

[save](javascript:void(0))

Artificial intelligence analysis of millions of dental radiographs has revealed substantially higher levels of untreated caries than reported by conventional public health surveys. (Image: LuxeShutter25/peopleimages.com/Adobe Stock)

[Dental Tribune International](https://www.dental-tribune.com/)

Mon. 10 August 2026

share

[save](javascript:void(0))

## LOS ANGELES, US: Dental AI company Pearl has released the Pearl Oral Health Index, which it describes as the first large-scale radiographic census of oral health in the US. Based on artificial intelligence (AI) analysis of millions of dental radiographs, the findings suggest that the burden of untreated caries may be substantially greater than previous national estimates. The analysis offers fresh insights into population oral health and highlights inequalities in access to dental care.

The index analysed radiographic data collected between April 2024 and March 2026 from more than 26 million dental visits involving approximately 15 million adults, covering around 737 million tooth observations. Using its AI technology—which has US Food and Drug Administration clearance—Pearl examined radiographic data at a scale not previously possible, creating what the company describes as the most comprehensive assessment of American oral health to date.

One of the report’s most striking findings is that untreated caries appears to be at least 4.5 times more common than the figure reported by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), which relies primarily on visual and tactile examinations of a nationally representative sample. Also, the average number of decayed teeth per patient identified by Pearl’s AI was 8.7 times that reported in NHANES. By comparison, the average numbers of missing and restored teeth closely matched government estimates, a similarity that Pearl argues lends credibility to its AI-based methodology.

The company argues that radiographs can reveal carious lesions that may not be detected using a visual and tactile examination, potentially explaining the discrepancy. This is consistent with [recent peer-reviewed research](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-16591-4) highlighting the value of radiographic examination for detecting hidden proximal caries and showing that AI can accurately identify caries involving enamel, dentine and pulp on panoramic radiographs, supporting the growing role of AI in improving radiographic diagnosis.

Beyond measuring disease prevalence, the analysis identified significant geographical inequalities. Among caries-affected teeth, extraction was about 40% more common in areas described as “dental deserts” than in better-served regions, reinforcing concerns that access to routine dental care remains uneven.

The report also uses UK data as a comparative lens and highlighted differences between the healthcare systems. It noted that treatment patterns varied between the US and the UK and suggested that funding models may influence whether severely damaged teeth are restored or extracted.

The findings illustrate how AI could transform population-level oral health surveillance by enabling radiographs to be analysed consistently at scale. Pearl suggests that the data could inform public health policy, dental education, insurance quality measures and future research, as well as provide a new benchmark against which improvements in oral health and access to care can be measured. Full details of the index can be accessed on [the Pearl website](https://hellopearl.com/oral-health-index).

The market growth is driven by the increasing adoption of digital dentistry, rising demand for accurate diagnosis, and expanding use of AI in imaging, orthodontics, and implant planning. Integration with CBCT, intraoral scanners, and CAD/CAM systems, along with workflow automation and improved treatment outcomes, is further driving market growth. In addition, the market is driven by the increasing collaborations between AI technology providers, dental device manufacturers, and oral healthcare companies to integrate AI into everyday clinical workflows. These partnerships enable continuous integration of AI with dental imaging systems, treatment planning software, and preventive care solutions, helping clinicians improve diagnostic accuracy, streamline workflows, and support evidence-based decision-making. AI-powered solutions are also enhancing patient communication, enabling earlier disease detection, and promoting minimally invasive treatment approaches. For instance, in August 2025, VideaHealth and vVARDIS expanded their collaboration to integrate AI-powered early caries detection with the drill-free Curodont Repair Fluoride Plus treatment. The integrated workflow has helped more than 400,000 patients receive early intervention for dental caries by enabling same-day diagnosis and treatment, improving preventive care adoption, and demonstrating the growing role of AI in routine clinical practice. “We founded VideaHealth to bring clinical clarity and consistency to every dental visit. This partnership demonstrates what’s possible when AI is used to strengthen and not replace clinical decision-making,” said Florian Hillen, CEO of VideaHealth. “In our collaboration with vVARDIS, we’re helping to create a world where early detection and drill-free treatment are the standards rather than the exception.” U.S. FDA Regulatory Approvals for AI-Based Dental Devices (2021-2026): Date of Final Decision Submission Number Device Company Panel (Lead) 3/5/2026 K252538 CEPHX3D Orca Dental AI, Ltd. Radiology 9/19/2025 K251002 Videa Dental AI VideaHealth Inc. Radiology 5/17/2024 DEN230035 DentalMonitoring Dental Monitoring SAS Dental 5/16/2024 K233625 RAYDENT SW RAY Co., Ltd. Dental 2/21/2024 K232148 X-Guide Surgical Navigation System X-Nav Technologies, LLC Dental 1/31/2024 K231396 CEPHX - Cephalometric Analysis Software Orca Dental AI Ltd. Radiology 12/15/2023 K232384 Videa Dental Assist VideaHealth, Inc. Radiology 5/19/2021 K210187 Overjet Dental Assist Overjet, Inc. Radiology Source: U.S.FDA The table highlights major U.S. FDA-cleared AI devices for the dentistry market between 2021 and 2026, showcasing advancements in AI-powered dental diagnostics, orthodontic monitoring, cephalometric analysis, imaging software, and implant navigation. These regulatory clearances demonstrate the increasing adoption of artificial intelligence in clinical dentistry, supporting improved diagnostic accuracy, treatment planning, workflow efficiency, and patient outcomes across diverse dental applications. Traditional dentistry relies on manual interpretation of dental images, clinician experience, and paper- or software-based documentation, which can result in variability in diagnosis, longer treatment planning, and inconsistent clinical outcomes. In contrast, AI-powered dentistry leverages technologies such as deep learning, computer vision, and cloud-based platforms to automate image analysis, support treatment planning, standardize diagnostic decisions, streamline documentation, and enhance patient communication. These capabilities improve diagnostic accuracy, operational efficiency, and workflow integration while enabling remote monitoring and more personalized dental care. AI-Driven Oral Health Insights from the Pearl Oral Health Index: Category Key Findings (2026) Study Overview Pearl analyzed 26 million dental X-rays, 15 million patients, and 737 million individual teeth, creating the first large-scale radiographic census of U.S. oral health. Untreated Dental Decay AI analysis found that untreated dental decay is 4.5× higher than estimates reported by the U.S. CDC NHANES survey. Decay Detection Average decayed teeth per patient were Pearl 6.07 compared with 0.7 reported by NHANES, representing an 8.7× higher detection rate. Missing Teeth Validation Pearl reported 2.16 missing teeth per patient, closely matching NHANES (2.0), validating the AI methodology. Restored Teeth Average restored teeth per patient reached 7.01, closely aligned with NHANES (6.0). Young Adults (18-24 Years) More than 52% of dental disease remained untreated, representing the highest level of untreated disease among all age groups. Older Adults (75+ Years) Individuals aged 75 years and older had 19.14 affected teeth (out of 28), while only 28% of disease remained untreated, indicating greater treatment management. Lowest Disease Burden Hawaii recorded the lowest disease burden with 9.63 affected teeth and the lowest calculus prevalence (45.0%). Highest Disease Burden Delaware showed the highest disease burden with 14.22 affected teeth and 62.6% calculus prevalence. Highest Tooth Extraction Rate Kansas reported the highest extraction rate, with nearly 1 in 10 affected teeth extracted rather than restored. Practice Diagnostic Variation AI identified a 4× variation in detected affected teeth between high- and low-diagnosing dental practices (12.4 vs. 3.1 teeth per patient). Gender-Based Dental Visits Women represented 56.2% of dental patients compared with 43.8% for men, indicating women were 28% more likely to visit a dentist. U.S. vs. U.K. Comparison U.S. patients averaged 2.16 missing teeth, compared with 6.36 in the U.K. The extraction rate was 14.5% in the U.S. versus ~31% in the U.K., reflecting differences in healthcare systems. Source: Pearl Inc. Market Dynamics The AI in dentistry market is experiencing strong growth due to the increasing adoption of digital dentistry and the rising demand for accurate, efficient, and standardized diagnosis. AI-powered solutions are transforming dental workflows by enabling automated image analysis, early disease detection, clinical decision support, and personalized treatment planning across specialties such as orthodontics, implantology, endodontics, periodontics, and restorative dentistry. The market is further driven by the integration of AI with CBCT systems, intraoral scanners, CAD/CAM platforms, electronic dental records, and cloud-based practice management software, improving workflow efficiency and patient outcomes. In addition, the growing prevalence of oral diseases, increasing investments in digital dental infrastructure, expansion of DSOs, and continuous advancements in machine learning, computer vision, and generative AI are expected to support sustained market growth during the forecast period. Driver: Rising adoption of AI-assisted dental imaging The increasing adoption of AI-assisted dental imaging is a major driver of the AI in dentistry market. Dental clinics and hospitals are integrating AI with digital imaging systems such as CBCT, panoramic X-rays, and intraoral radiography to improve diagnostic accuracy and clinical efficiency. AI automatically detects dental caries, periodontal bone loss, periapical lesions, and other oral abnormalities, reducing interpretation time and supporting evidence-based treatment planning. AI also enhances consistency across clinicians and improves patient communication through visual diagnostic reports. Restraint: Limited availability of high-quality dental datasets The limited availability of large, diverse, and high-quality annotated dental datasets remains a significant restraint for the AI in dentistry market. AI models require extensive clinical data from different populations, imaging systems, and dental conditions to achieve reliable performance. However, variations in image quality, inconsistent annotation standards, fragmented data sources, and patient privacy regulations restrict access to comprehensive datasets. These challenges can reduce algorithm accuracy, limit generalizability across clinical settings, and increase the time and cost required for AI development, validation, and regulatory approval, particularly for smaller AI developers. Opportunity: Expansion of AI in preventive dentistry The growing focus on preventive and minimally invasive dentistry presents a significant opportunity for AI in dentistry market. AI enables the early detection of dental caries, periodontal disease, and other oral conditions before they progress, allowing clinicians to provide timely preventive treatment and improve long-term oral health outcomes. Increasing awareness of preventive dental care, combined with the expansion of digital dentistry in emerging economies, is expected to accelerate AI adoption. Market Concentration & Characteristics The AI in dentistry market is characterized by a high degree of innovation, driven by rapid advancements in machine learning, computer vision, generative AI, and cloud-based digital dentistry. AI is integrated with CBCT systems, intraoral scanners, CAD/CAM platforms, and practice management software to create connected digital workflows. For instance, in May 2025, Pearl became the first dental AI company to receive FDA clearance for both 2D and 3D dental image analysis, extending AI capabilities to CBCT imaging and strengthening AI-assisted diagnosis in dental practices. “Pearl’s mission has always been to deliver the most advanced and clinically trusted AI solutions in dentistry,” said Ophir Tanz, founder and CEO of Pearl. “Becoming the first company to achieve FDA clearance for both 2D and 3D radiologic analysis isn’t just a milestone for us-it’s a milestone for dentistry.” The AI in dentistry market has witnessed moderate to high strategic collaboration, partnership, and acquisition activity as companies expand their AI-enabled digital dentistry portfolios. AI developers are partnering with imaging companies, dental software providers, and DSOs to integrate AI into routine clinical workflows. For instance, in September 2025, Dentsply Sirona partnered with Pearl to integrate Pearl’s Second Opinion AI software into the DS Core cloud platform, enabling AI-assisted analysis of 2D dental X-rays. The collaboration enhanced radiologic support by improving detection of conditions such as early-stage caries and bone loss while strengthening patient communication through AI-generated visual annotations and measurements. “This collaboration with Dentsply Sirona brings our vision of accessible, trustworthy dental AI to an even broader global audience,” said Ophir Tanz, CEO of Pearl. “By embedding Second Opinion directly into DS Core, we’re giving clinicians seamless access to AI insights that strengthen their diagnostic confidence, improve patient communication, and ultimately elevate the standard of care across every practice.” AI-powered dental software is regulated as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), making regulatory approval a critical factor for commercialization. Manufacturers must comply with requirements related to clinical validation, algorithm performance, cybersecurity, data privacy, quality management systems, and post-market monitoring. In major markets, AI solutions require regulatory clearance before commercial deployment. The AI in dentistry market faces moderate competition from traditional diagnostic methods, manual radiographic interpretation, and conventional dental software without AI functionality. Many dental practices continue to rely on clinician expertise for image interpretation and treatment planning, particularly where digital infrastructure is limited. However, AI offers significant advantages by improving diagnostic consistency, reducing interpretation time, supporting clinical decision-making, and enhancing patient communication. As digital dentistry adoption increases, AI-enabled solutions are gradually replacing conventional manual workflows in advanced dental practices. Demand for AI in dentistry solutions is highly concentrated among dental clinics, multispecialty dental hospitals, DSOs, specialty dental centers, and academic institutions. Organizations with high patient volumes and advanced digital infrastructure are the primary adopters because AI improves diagnostic consistency, workflow efficiency, and treatment planning. Large DSOs are deploying AI across multiple locations to standardize clinical decision-making. For instance, in June 2026, Smile Brands partnered with Pearl to deploy its Radiographic AI platform across its dental network following a successful pilot. The rollout improved diagnostic consistency, patient communication, and same-day treatment acceptance, supporting higher-quality dental care. Analyst Perspective The AI in dentistry market is expected to grow steadily, driven by the increasing adoption of digital dentistry, rising demand for accurate diagnosis, and growing use of AI-powered imaging and treatment planning solutions. AI is being widely adopted in dental radiology, orthodontics, implantology, and restorative dentistry to improve diagnostic accuracy, automate image analysis, and support clinical decision-making. The market is also benefiting from greater integration of AI with CBCT systems, intraoral scanners, CAD/CAM platforms, and practice management software. Increasing investments in digital dental infrastructure and the expansion of specialty dental clinics are further supporting market growth. Companies that offer clinically validated, easy-to-use, and interoperable AI solutions while ensuring regulatory compliance, data security, and seamless workflow integration will be well positioned to strengthen their market presence and achieve long-term growth. Solution Type Insights The AI-powered diagnostic software segment dominated the AI in dentistry market, accounting for 42.0% of the market in 2025. This dominance is supported by the growing adoption of AI-assisted radiographic analysis, increasing demand for early and accurate detection of dental diseases, widespread integration with digital imaging systems, rising FDA-cleared diagnostic solutions, and the need to improve clinical efficiency, diagnostic consistency, and treatment planning. For instance, in March 2025, Align Technology launched Align X-ray Insights across the European Union and the UK, an AI-powered computer-aided detection (CADe) software that automatically analyzes 2D dental radiographs. The solution enhances diagnostic accuracy and supports more efficient clinical decision-making in digital dentistry. The AI-powered patient communication & engagement software segment in the AI in dentistry market is expected to grow at the fastest rate during the forecast period due to the increasing adoption of AI-driven patient engagement platforms, automated appointment scheduling, personalized treatment communication, virtual assistants, multilingual support, and digital follow-up solutions that enhance patient experience, improve treatment acceptance, and strengthen practice efficiency. For instance, in August 2025, 3Shape launched the TRIOS 6 intraoral scanner with AI-assisted Dx Plus diagnostic software to enhance dental examinations through AI-powered diagnostics. The solution improves disease detection, streamlines diagnostic workflows, and strengthens communication between dentists and patients. Technology Insights The computer vision segment dominated the AI in dentistry market, accounting for 31.4% of the market in 2025. This dominance is supported by the widespread preference for AI-assisted dental image analysis, increasing adoption of digital radiography and CBCT systems, growing use of automated detection of caries and periodontal diseases, and the integration of computer vision algorithms into diagnostic, orthodontic, and treatment planning workflows to improve accuracy and clinical efficiency. The generative AI segment in the AI in dentistry market is expected to grow at the fastest rate during the forecast period due to the increasing adoption of AI-powered clinical documentation, automated treatment recommendations, patient communication tools, personalized treatment planning, report generation, and workflow automation. Growing investments in cloud-based AI platforms and the integration of generative AI into dental practice management systems are further accelerating segment growth. For instance, in December 2024, the American Dental Association (ADA) made a strategic investment in Pearl's dental AI platform to support the advancement of AI in dentistry. The investment highlights the ADA's commitment to accelerating AI-driven innovations that improve diagnostic accuracy, patient care, and clinical outcomes. Clinical Application Insights The general dentistry segment dominated the AI in dentistry market, accounting for 31.8% of the market in 2025. This dominance is supported by the widespread use of AI for routine dental examinations, radiographic interpretation, caries detection, periodontal disease assessment, and treatment planning. Increasing adoption of digital imaging systems, growing patient volumes, and the need for improved diagnostic accuracy and workflow efficiency have further strengthened the segment's market position. The implant dentistry segment in the AI in dentistry market is expected to grow at the fastest rate during the forecast period due to the increasing demand for dental implants, rising adoption of CBCT-guided implant planning, AI-assisted 3D anatomical analysis, surgical navigation technologies, and digital treatment planning. The company raised $60 million in Series B funding in 2025 led by Oak HC/FT with participation from Greco, SNR, and existing investors, and has hired new executives including a former Goldman Sachs engineer and the co-founder of Pearl who helped build the world's first FDA-cleared dental AI medical device. Artifical Intelligence/Machine Learning A Growing Akido Calls Itself ‘First AI-Native Health System’ in U.S. Company is expanding its proprietary technology, ScopeAI, across its 100 clinics, virtual care, and field medicine services in California, New York City, and Rhode Island





Courtesy of Akido In California, Akido’s tech-supported care model is bolstering street medicine programs.

A February 2026 Healthcare Innovation article focused on how several California-based organizations are coming together to use AI technology and community health workers to bolster street medicine programs. The initiative uses the tech-supported care model of Akido Labs, which was founded in 2015 out of USC's Digital Health Lab. Acknowledging that it has moved past the R&D phase, Akido has now dropped the "Labs," from its name, becoming simply Akido. The company said it is building the first “AI-native health system” in the United States, expanding its proprietary technology, ScopeAI, across its 100 clinics, virtual care, and field medicine services, with access to a population of 1 million patients in California, New York City, and Rhode Island.



In 2025 the company raised $60 million in Series B funding. The round was led by Oak HC/FT with participation from Greco, SNR, and existing investors Y Combinator, Future Communities Capital, Jeff Dean (Chief Scientist, Google DeepMind & Google Research), and the Comprehensive Blood & Cancer Center. Prashant Samant is the company's co-founder & CEO. Akido says its ScopeAI listens during the visit, organizes the clinical picture in real time, and hands the physician a diagnostic head start.



Matt Siegler is Akido’s chief network officer. Previously he served in roles at Kaiser Permanente and most recently as chief growth and strategy officer at NYC Health & Hospitals. Street medicine providers are a special breed, Siegler told Healthcare Innovation earlier this year. It’s difficult to find people who are committed enough to do this work, and it's difficult to sustain the work, he said. “You have to enable people and support them with a broad team of caregivers. You have to provide them with ways to reach these patients and follow up on their needs in an ongoing way. Doing that with paper and pen and physically out in the street every day as an M.D., going from tent to tent or shelter to shelter, can be very challenging and is not sustainable from a financial perspective for most providers,” he added.



Akido’s model involves enabling community health workers and others with lived experience and cultural competency to reach people. The information they gather is sent to the physician’s device and they review it. They can then order through the EHR and decide the next step that the patient needs in their journey. Its use of technology paired with the clinical rigor and commitment to do this work is what Siegler says is the secret sauce. “Lots of people have technology, but they don't want to deploy it for this population.”



Akido also announced a few other new execs. Matt Rothstein joined as vice president of engineering. At Goldman Sachs, he was integral to building the Apple Card platform, stood up Goldman's first real-time ML model in consumer, and scaled engineering from 10 to 250 people. He previously built patient record transfer systems at the National Institutes of Health and an ED charting system used across seven hospitals in Maryland.



Cambron Carter joined as principal AI architect. Co-founder and former Chief Technology Officer of Pearl, he built a 60-person engineering team and co-led regulatory submissions for the world's first FDA-cleared dental AI medical device.



Akido has launched an AI Clinical Advisory Council, an independent panel of clinicians, health equity voices, payer leaders, and patient advocates providing external oversight of Akido's AI systems and protocols. Dental offices now use AI software for more than reviewing images, weaving it into daily work such as booking appointments, recording visits, processing insurance claims, and communicating with patients, while dentists still make all final clinical decisions. What Is Changing in How Practices Specify AI Software? Dental offices are using software to send reminders, confirm visits, fill open slots, and follow up with patients who miss appointments, protecting daily income against empty chair time. Billing staff use the same tools to check insurance coverage, prepare claims, and follow up on rejections, and dentists are more likely to adopt clinical AI when staff can review its work, track changes, and correct mistakes. Which Deployments and Functions Lead the Market? Cloud-based deployment leads at about 38.3% share, supported by browser access, automatic updates, and shared use across several locations, ahead of on-premise and hybrid models. Appointment scheduling and automation tops AI-function demand at roughly 25%, since a missed visit leaves a chair empty and cuts daily income, and practice management leads application demand at close to 30% by bringing appointments, records, billing, and daily reports into one system. Solo dental practices place about 30% of end-user demand. Which Countries Present the Strongest Growth? Germany leads at a 23.1% CAGR through 2036 on better appointment control and chair-utilisation planning, with Brazil close behind at 21.4% on billing automation and multi-site workflows. The United States follows at 19.7% on dental-group growth and insurance processing, ahead of South Korea (18.0%), the United Kingdom (16.2%), and Japan (14.5%). What Could Slow Adoption? Clinical-control and human-override requirements are the main brake, since practices may avoid AI tools when dentists cannot see how a result was created or changed, and each system needs simple review and rejection steps. Unreliable or poorly governed generative AI outputs add a second constraint, as inaccurate notes or suggestions increase the chance that wrong information enters a patient record or message. How Are Suppliers Responding? Henry Schein One and Planet DDS lead through wide dental practice software ranges, with Henry Schein One announcing AWS-backed generative AI work and Planet DDS pairing cloud practice software with Pearl39s AI image review. Carestream Dental and Curve Dental provide cloud software and imaging links, while Denti.AI, VideaHealth, Pearl, and Overjet focus more narrowly on clinical and imaging AI. Competition centres on how well tasks work together and whether automation keeps the dentist in control. What Should Practices and DSOs Monitor Through 2036? Separate tasks the software handles on its own from those requiring staff review, and confirm a simple correction process exists for fixing wrong results. Test any new setup at a few locations before applying it across a larger group, and confirm data security, data ownership, service support, and export options in customer agreements before committing to one software company. DENVER, July 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- INFLUENCE élevé Magazine will debut its exclusive Dykema 2026 Special Issue at the 13th Annual Dykema DSO Conference, bringing together leading voices, innovators, and organizations helping shape the future of dentistry.

The dual cover features Brian Colao, Director of Dykema's DSO Industry Group, and Ophir Tanz, Founder and CEO of Pearl, whose insights highlight two of the profession's defining conversations: the evolution of the business of dentistry and the responsible integration of artificial intelligence into patient care.

At a time when dentistry is being transformed by technology, the greatest competitive advantage may still be the people behind it. Beyond technology and business strategy, the special issue explores leadership, innovation, philanthropy, personal growth, and the people driving meaningful change across the profession.

Featured contributors include Brian Colao, Director of Dykema's DSO Industry Group; Ophir Tanz, Founder and CEO of Pearl; Amol Nirgudkar, Co-Founder and CEO of Patient Prism; Dr. Farzeela Rupani, Chief Medical Officer of Colosseum Dental Group; Rob Woolley, CEO of HuFriedyGroup; Jeff Wheeler, Co-Founder and CEO of Children's Surgery Centers; a special tribute honoring the legacy of Pat Bauer; and additional industry leaders from across the dental profession.

The Dykema 2026 Special Issue also features organizations including Pearl, Patient Prism, Henry Schein One, Weave, Tower Leadership, Rise DDS, RipeGlobal, Zentist, and Kwikly, highlighting innovations in artificial intelligence, interoperability, patient acquisition, workforce development, practice growth, and emerging technologies.

Inside the issue, Brian Colao examines the unprecedented economic pressures facing dentistry while outlining why innovation and strategic technology adoption have become essential to long-term success.

"Leveraging technology is no longer optional—it is essential for the success of any dental organization in 2026. Doing things the way they have always been done and hoping for the best is no longer effective in the current environment," said Brian Colao, Director of Dykema's DSO Industry Group.

Ophir Tanz explores the relationship between artificial intelligence and craftsmanship, arguing that technology should reduce friction and administrative complexity while allowing clinicians to devote more time to the uniquely human aspects of dentistry.

"Dentistry and woodworking are very similar. There's a set of tools, and then there's the craft of using them well," said Ophir Tanz, Founder and CEO of Pearl.

Complimentary print copies of the Dykema 2026 Special Issue will be available beginning July 15 at the Dykema DSO Conference while supplies last. The digital edition will also be released on July 15, 2026. Subscribers may access the issue at:

https://influentialdental.co/magazine/

Published by Influential Holdings, Inc., INFLUENCE élevé Magazine, co-founded by Julieanne O'Connor and Michael Keeter, is the first lifestyle and mindset magazine created exclusively for dental professionals, covering leadership, mindset, innovation, entrepreneurship, personal growth, and the people shaping the future of dentistry.

data.ai_summary: Pearl, an AI-driven healthcare startup, raised $110 million in funding. data.full_text:
Yapay zeka destekli sağlık girişimi Pearl, 110 milyon dolar yatırım aldı. Şirketin 110 milyon dolarlık yatırım turu iki farklı finansman yapısından oluştu.

Yatırımın 50 milyon dolarlık bölümü Andreessen Horowitz liderliğinde gerçekleşen öz sermaye yatırım turundan geldi. Bu yatırım turunda Viking Global Investors, AlleyCorp ve Ulysses Capital yer aldı. Yatırımın kalan 60 milyon dolarlık kısmı ise Trinity Capital tarafından sağlanan borç finansmanı olarak gerçekleşti.

Pearl, yeni gelen yatırımı yapay zeka platformunu geliştirmek, sağlık sistemi ve sigorta kuruluşlarıyla iş birliklerini büyütmek ve yeni risk yönetimi çözümleri geliştirmek için kullanacağını açıkladı.

Şirket, 2020 yılında Michael Kopko, Jeffrey DeFlavio, Ankit Patel ve Kevin Ryan tarafından hayata geçirildi. Pearl, Medicare hastalarına hizmet veren sağlık kuruluşları ve doktorlar için yapay zeka destekli bir sağlık teknolojisi platformu geliştiriyor. Platform, hastaların sağlık risklerini analiz ederek bakım süreçlerinin daha etkili yönetilmesine yardımcı oluyor.

Pearl'ün geliştirdiği sistem, sağlık hizmeti sağlayıcılarının iş akışlarını düzenliyor, riskleri önceden tahmin ediyor ve olası sağlık sorunları büyümeden önce gerekli adımların atılmasını otomatikleştiriyor. Böylece hem bakım kalitesinin artırılması hem de sağlık maliyetlerinin azaltılması hedefleniyor.

Şirket, ayrıca yapay zeka ajanlarıyla yıllık sağlık kontrollerinin planlanması, taburcu olduktan sonra hasta takibi ve bakım yönetimi gibi idari süreçleri otomatikleştirerek sağlık çalışanlarının hastalara daha fazla zaman ayırmasını sağlıyor.

Alpha Partners backs Pearl in historic $58 million dental AI funding round

We are excited to announce our participation in Pearl’s groundbreaking $58 million Series B funding round, the largest ever investment in dental artificial intelligence. This investment solidifies Pearl’s position as a global leader in revolutionizing dental care through AI-powered solutions. Elevating dental care standards Pearl’s AI technology is transforming the dental industry by addressing a key challenge: inconsistent diagnostic accuracy. By leveraging machine learning and computer vision, Pearl’s platform serves as a real-time aid for dentists, enhancing the accuracy and consistency of X-ray interpretations, ultimately improving patient care. This translates to increased efficiency within dental clinics and dental service organizations, as dentists can spend less time reviewing X-rays and more time providing care. On average, Pearl’s AI has also been shown to boost patient acceptance of recommended treatments by 30%. Additionally, the AI tool has proven valuable for insurers by reducing fraud, waste, and abuse. With FDA clearance and regulatory authorizations in over 120 countries, Pearl’s impact spans six continents. This significant investment will fuel further innovation, allowing Pearl to expand their product line, strengthen their intellectual property, and make AI-powered dental care accessible to an even wider audience. The Alpha Partners model Alpha Partners is a $150 million growth fund writing $3-$15 million checks into primary venture rounds. Our model is to partner with companies’ early investors and help them continue to bet on their winning portfolio companies by leveraging their access to new financings. We have built a deep network of 1000+ investment firms that spans early, growth, and pre-IPO investors, and to date have deployed over $250 million into 30 companies with this strategy. If you’d like to discuss collaborating with Alpha, please reach out to hello@alphapartners.com or livechat us via our website. We are honored to join Left Lane Capital, Smash Capital, Craft Ventures, Neotribe Ventures, and Crosscut Ventures in supporting Pearl.

data.title: The Pearl Oral Health Index Delivers the First Radiographic Census of the American Mouth
data.ai_summary: Pearl, a dental AI company, released its Oral Health Index providing the first radiographic census of American oral health by analyzing 1.49 million full-mouth x-ray series and 14.8 million patient encounters across the U.S. and U.K. The study found significant geographic disparities, with Hawaii showing the lowest disease burden (9.63 affected teeth per patient) versus Delaware at 14.22, and revealed that dental deserts—zip codes with zero dentists—experience 40 percent higher tooth extraction rates compared to areas with 51+ dentists. The index also demonstrates a stark contrast between dental systems, showing U.S. patients average 2.16 missing teeth versus 6.36 for U.K. patients, reflecting how fee-for-service insurance incentivizes restoration while NHS budget constraints favor extraction.

Article content The Geography of the American Mouth

Where a person lives shapes not just whether they get sick, but what happens when they do. A look at the states with the best and worst oral health include: Article content Lowest disease burden: Hawaii (9.63 teeth showing signs of decay, loss, or restoration; lowest calculus at 45.0 percent; fewest extractions).

Highest disease burden: Delaware (14.22 showing signs of decay, loss, or restoration; calculus 62.6 percent).

Highest tartar buildup: New Jersey (67.7 percent of patients). This is a 23-point spread vs. Hawaii on a single hygiene indicator.

Highest rate of extraction: Kansas, where nearly 1 in 10 affected teeth was extracted rather than restored. Article content The Dentist Lottery: A 4x gap in what two offices on the same block may diagnose

Across 282 dental offices each seeing 200+ adult patients, the 10th-percentile practice finds 3.1 affected teeth per patient, while the 90th-percentile practice finds 12.4 — a 4x gap. Within single zip codes, Pearl identified a 9.2 percentage-point average spread in D-Load (the share of decay left untreated) between neighboring offices, with the top 10 percent of zip codes showing spreads of 17.8 points. Pearl’s AI analyzed every x-ray; what varied was how practices responded to what it found. This is not a disease gap, rather it is a training, awareness, and diagnostic consistency gap. Article content Article content Dental Deserts: Patients in zip codes with zero dentists lose 40 percent more teeth

Pearl matched zip-code data against the National Provider Identifier (NPI) registry of 180,974 U.S. dental practices and 295,509 dentists. In zip codes with zero dentists, 20.8 percent of affected teeth have been extracted. In zip codes with 51+ dentists, only 14.9 percent are extracted, which marks a 40 percent higher rate of tooth loss in so-called dental deserts. Patients in these communities are not going untreated longer; when they finally receive care, they lose the tooth entirely, which often comes down to affordability. In many cases prevention and treatment comes at a higher cost than extraction. Article content The Access Signal: American women are 28 percent more likely to visit a dentist than men

In the U.S. dataset, women make up 56.2 percent of patients and men 43.8 percent. Under the U.K.’s National Health Service (NHS), the split is exactly 50/50. Once men and women are in the chair, their clinical numbers are remarkably similar (e.g. female’s untreated rate of 31.4 percent vs. male 33.9 percent). The real gap is not in the mouth — though men do have a higher rate of calculus (1.99 vs. 1.67), or teeth with tartar build up, whereas women tend to have more fillings (7.97 vs. 7.37) — it’s in who makes it through the door. The data shows that when disease is found, Americans restore and the British extract: Article content U.S. patients average 2.16 missing teeth. U.K. patients average 6.36 — roughly 3x more.

In the U.S. the share of affected teeth extracted sits at 14.5 percent whereas in the U.K. that number’s ~31 percent. Article content U.S. fee-for-service insurance incentivizes restoration; in the U.K., NHS budget constraints make extraction the more accessible option when a tooth is severely compromised. Neither is objectively superior. But the radiographic evidence shows the two systems produce fundamentally different outcomes in peoples’ mouths. Article content Why This Matters Now

Oral health is among the last corners of American medicine to be digitized, standardized, and studied at scale. The Pearl Oral Health Index closes that gap in a single step. By applying a consistent, FDA-cleared AI detection model to this volume of x-rays, Pearl has produced the first objective, comparable, population-level picture of what is actually happening inside millions of mouths and how various dental systems respond to it.

This is the authoritative source for DMF (average 15.24 of 28 teeth affected, composed of 6.07 decayed, 2.16 missing and 7.01 filled). Its missing-teeth figure matches NHANES almost exactly, validating the methodology.

data.ai_summary: Pearl, a dental AI company, released the Pearl Oral Health Index, analyzing 26 million dental x-rays across 15 million patients and 737 million teeth to produce the largest radiographic census of American oral health. The study found that U.S. cavity rates are 4.5 times worse than CDC NHANES estimates, with 94 percent of adults aged 18-24 having untreated dental disease and patients in "dental deserts" losing 40 percent more teeth than those in areas with sufficient dental coverage. data.full_text:
The Index analyzes 737 million teeth across 15 million patients and 26 million dental x-rays

Reveals America’s cavity problem is 4.5x worse than government data indicate

Identifies and quantifies the impact in America’s “dental deserts” where the tooth-loss gap exceeds 40 percent





LOS ANGELES, June 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Pearl , the global leader in dental AI solutions, today released the Pearl Oral Health Index , unlocking key insights across age, location, gender, and more in the most comprehensive radiographic census of American oral health ever produced. Using its FDA-cleared AI platform to read dental x-rays at scale, Pearl analyzed more than 26 million dental x-rays across 15 million unique patients, and 737 million individual teeth. This represents a dataset so vast it has, for the first time in history, made the collective reality of the American mouth legible. The data both reveals and challenges assumptions about who gets sick, who gets treated, and why.

Until now, dental research has largely relied on small-sample surveys. X-rays, which are the single richest source of oral health information, have been locked away in tens of millions of isolated patient files, impossible to aggregate or compare. Pearl is the first dental AI platform to read, analyze, and measure them at population scale.

“For the first time, we can see what's actually happening inside the mouths of America, not through a survey, not through a sample, but through the raw radiographic truth of tens of millions of visits,” said Ophir Tanz, founder and CEO, Pearl. “The picture is dramatically different from what the public data has told us for decades. There is more disease, more inequality, and more variability in care than anyone realized. AI didn't create this problem, but it finally let us measure it.”

Key Findings

The X-Ray Gap: America's cavity problem is at least 4.5 times worse than federal data suggests

The CDC's NHANES, the gold-standard U.S. government oral health survey of just 25,000 participants, uses mirrors and probes in mobile clinics and estimates that roughly 21 percent of American adults have untreated decay. Pearl's AI, reading radiographs of 15 million participants, finds the real figure is at least 4.5 times higher.

Decayed teeth per patient: Pearl 6.07 vs. NHANES 0.7. This reflects an 8.7x gap in detected decay.

Missing teeth per patient: Pearl 2.16 vs. NHANES 2.0. This near-perfect match gives credence to Pearl's methodology, since empty sockets are visible to both a probe and an x-ray.

Restored teeth per patient: Pearl 7.01 vs. NHANES 6.0. Like missing teeth, restorations are generally visible to the naked eye, so the near-alignment here likewise supports Pearl’s methodology.





X-rays can reveal demineralization at 30–60 percent mineral loss, which is well before a cavity is visible to the eye. The difference is not a methodological quirk; it is the cost of measuring the nation's oral health with instruments that were state-of-the-art in the 19th century. Of note, everyone in Pearl's dataset was already in a dental chair, meaning the true spread in the general population is likely even higher.

Young adults have the most neglected mouths; older adults have the most managed

Ages 18–24: 52 percent or more than half of all dental disease in young adults is untreated. These are the most neglected mouths in the dataset.

Crossover between ages 35–44: Fillings finally overtake untreated decay. This is when most people evolve from neglect to managing their oral health.

Ages 75+: The number of teeth showing signs of decay, loss, or restoration rises to 19.14 out of 28 teeth, meaning over two thirds of teeth have had an issue. Only 28 percent of that damage is untreated. By the time a person hits 75 years old, their mouth is not healthier, but it is more managed.





The Geography of the American Mouth

Where a person lives shapes not just whether they get sick, but what happens when they do. A look at the states with the best and worst oral health include:

Lowest disease burden: Hawaii (9.63 teeth showing signs of decay, loss, or restoration; lowest calculus at 45.0 percent; fewest extractions).

Highest disease burden: Delaware (14.22 showing signs of decay, loss, or restoration; calculus 62.6 percent).

Highest tartar buildup: New Jersey (67.7 percent of patients). This is a 23-point spread vs. Hawaii on a single hygiene indicator.

Highest rate of extraction: Kansas, where nearly 1 in 10 affected teeth was extracted rather than restored.





The Dentist Lottery: A 4x gap in what two offices on the same block may diagnose

Across 282 dental offices each seeing 200+ adult patients, the 10th-percentile practice finds 3.1 affected teeth per patient, while the 90th-percentile practice finds 12.4 — a 4x gap. Within single zip codes, Pearl identified a 9.2 percentage-point average spread in D-Load (the share of decay left untreated) between neighboring offices, with the top 10 percent of zip codes showing spreads of 17.8 points. Pearl's AI analyzed every x-ray; what varied was how practices responded to what it found. This is not a disease gap, rather it is a training, awareness, and diagnostic consistency gap.

Dental Deserts: Patients in zip codes with zero dentists lose 40 percent more teeth

Pearl matched zip-code data against the National Provider Identifier (NPI) registry of 180,974 U.S. dental practices and 295,509 dentists. In zip codes with zero dentists, 20.8 percent of affected teeth have been extracted. In zip codes with 51+ dentists, only 14.9 percent are extracted, which marks a 40 percent higher rate of tooth loss in so-called dental deserts. Patients in these communities are not going untreated longer; when they finally receive care, they lose the tooth entirely, which often comes down to affordability. In many cases prevention and treatment comes at a higher cost than extraction.

The Access Signal: American women are 28 percent more likely to visit a dentist than men

In the U.S. dataset, women make up 56.2 percent of patients and men 43.8 percent. Under the U.K.'s National Health Service (NHS), the split is exactly 50/50. Once men and women are in the chair, their clinical numbers are remarkably similar (e.g. female’s untreated rate of 31.4 percent vs. male 33.9 percent). The real gap is not in the mouth — though men do have a higher rate of calculus (1.99 vs. 1.67), or teeth with tartar build up, whereas women tend to have more fillings (7.97 vs. 7.37) — it’s in who makes it through the door.

Two Countries, Two Dental Systems, Two Completely Different Mouths

The data shows that when disease is found, Americans restore and the British extract:

U.S. patients average 2.16 missing teeth. U.K. patients average 6.36 — roughly 3x more.

In the U.S. the share of affected teeth extracted sits at 14.5 percent whereas in the U.K. that number’s ~31 percent.





U.S. fee-for-service insurance incentivizes restoration; in the U.K., NHS budget constraints make extraction the more accessible option when a tooth is severely compromised. Neither is objectively superior. But the radiographic evidence shows the two systems produce fundamentally different outcomes in peoples’ mouths.

Why This Matters Now

Oral health is among the last corners of American medicine to be digitized, standardized, and studied at scale. The Pearl Oral Health Index closes that gap in a single step. By applying a consistent, FDA-cleared AI detection model to this volume of x-rays, Pearl has produced the first objective, comparable, population-level picture of what is actually happening inside millions of mouths and how various dental systems respond to it.

The Index's findings have immediate implications for public-health policy, insurer quality metrics, dental-school curricula, and patient expectations. And it establishes a new baseline against which every future change, including new therapies, new policies, and expanded access, can be measured.

About the Data

The Pearl Oral Health Index draws on two complementary datasets, both covering adults 18+, all 51 U.S. states (including D.C.) and the U.K., using a 28-tooth universe (excluding wisdom teeth) across April 2024 to March 2026:

FMX Series Dataset: 1.49 million patients with complete full-mouth x-ray series analyzed by Pearl. This is the authoritative source for DMF (average 15.24 of 28 teeth affected, composed of 6.07 decayed, 2.16 missing and 7.01 filled). Its missing-teeth figure matches NHANES almost exactly, validating the methodology.

Expanded Encounters Dataset: 14.8 million patients and 26 million tooth-level dental encounters, powering state-level analyses, gender comparisons, tooth-by-tooth vulnerability timelines, and 4.26 million longitudinal tooth transitions.





You can access the full version of the Pearl Oral Health Index here: https://hellopearl.com/oral-health-index

About Pearl

Pearl is a dental AI company committed to enhancing how patient care is delivered. Founded in 2019 by a team with decades of experience developing successful, enterprise-grade computer vision solutions, Pearl introduced the first-ever FDA-cleared AI capable of reading and instantly identifying diseases in dental x-rays. With regulatory clearance in 120 countries, Pearl's AI assists dentists in making precise clinical decisions and effectively communicating with patients, thereby transforming the dental care experience worldwide. As dentistry’s global AI leader, Pearl is committed to the ongoing innovation of robust, accessible AI tools that improve patient health outcomes and build greater trust in dental medicine. To request a demo, please visit hellopearl.com/demo

The real gap is not in the mouth — though men do have a higher rate of calculus (1.99 vs. 1.67), or teeth with tartar build up, whereas women tend to have more fillings (7.97 vs. 7.37) — it’s in who makes it through the door. Two Countries, Two Dental Systems, Two Completely Different Mouths

The data shows that when disease is found, Americans restore and the British extract: U.S. patients average 2.16 missing teeth. U.K. patients average 6.36 — roughly 3x more.

In the U.S. the share of affected teeth extracted sits at 14.5 percent whereas in the U.K. that number’s ~31 percent.



U.S. fee-for-service insurance incentivizes restoration; in the U.K., NHS budget constraints make extraction the more accessible option when a tooth is severely compromised. Neither is objectively superior. But the radiographic evidence shows the two systems produce fundamentally different outcomes in peoples’ mouths. Why This Matters Now

Oral health is among the last corners of American medicine to be digitized, standardized, and studied at scale. The Pearl Oral Health Index closes that gap in a single step. By applying a consistent, FDA-cleared AI detection model to this volume of x-rays, Pearl has produced the first objective, comparable, population-level picture of what is actually happening inside millions of mouths and how various dental systems respond to it. The Index's findings have immediate implications for public-health policy, insurer quality metrics, dental-school curricula, and patient expectations. And it establishes a new baseline against which every future change, including new therapies, new policies, and expanded access, can be measured. About the Data

The Pearl Oral Health Index draws on two complementary datasets, both covering adults 18+, all 51 U.S. states (including D.C.) and the U.K., using a 28-tooth universe (excluding wisdom teeth) across April 2024 to March 2026: FMX Series Dataset: 1.49 million patients with complete full-mouth x-ray series analyzed by Pearl. This is the authoritative source for DMF (average 15.24 of 28 teeth affected, composed of 6.07 decayed, 2.16 missing and 7.01 filled). Its missing-teeth figure matches NHANES almost exactly, validating the methodology.

Expanded Encounters Dataset: 14.8 million patients and 26 million tooth-level dental encounters, powering state-level analyses, gender comparisons, tooth-by-tooth vulnerability timelines, and 4.26 million longitudinal tooth transitions.

data.title: Top AI Models Might Be Confident—Doesn’t Mean They’re Right
data.ai_summary: Pearl Enterprise evaluated leading AI models and found OpenAI's GPT-5.5 achieved 72.7% expert alignment overall, but its performance varied by domain, falling to 68.8% in health and 62.1% in pets. Executives argue that public benchmark scores do not prove a system is trustworthy in real-world enterprise work, where mistakes can be costly.

Companies buying AI are running into a central problem. Public benchmarks can show whether a system performs well on a standardized task. They are less useful for deciding whether the same system can be trusted inside a company’s own work, using its data, rules and oversight requirements. Pearl Enterprise, which builds AI systems for professional services, has put numbers around that concern. In a new evaluation of leading AI models, the company compared model responses with expert-authored answers across business, health, law, pets and technology. The top model, OpenAI’s GPT-5.5, reached 72.7 percent expert alignment overall, according to Pearl’s leaderboard. Andy Kurtzig, CEO of Pearl, said the result should change how executives hear claims about top-ranked AI systems. “A C- student who knows they’re a C- student is manageable,” Kurtzig told Newsweek. “A C- student who’s convinced they’re an A+ student, and answers every question with total confidence, is the one who gets a company in trouble.” Pearl’s findings need some context. The company sells AI systems for professional services, a category where expert review is central to the product. The leaderboard measures expert alignment, rather than a simple right-or-wrong score. According to Pearl’s public methodology, the AI models were given the same questions used to create expert reference answers, without tuning or post-processing. Their responses were then scored against those expert-authored answers on a 1-to-5 rubric using Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet model. Pearl is not the only company raising this sort of concern. Executives working across AI security, software, compliance and enterprise deployment told Newsweek that higher public scores do not prove a system is truly ready for work where mistakes can be costly. Rob Clark, president of Seekr, an AI company focused on model evaluation, said rankings can help companies compare systems, but they cannot substitute for testing a tool inside a specific business setting. “A leaderboard ranking is not a trust decision,” Clark told Newsweek. “Confidence scores measure how sure the model is, not how right it is.” Pearl’s domain results make the point more clearly when viewed within the same model. GPT-5.5 led the business category with 80.9 percent expert alignment, but Pearl’s data showed the same model falling to 68.8 percent in health and 62.1 percent in pets. The spread suggests companies need to ask a narrower question: whether a high-ranking model has been tested in the specific field where it will be used. Companies rarely deploy AI for “general intelligence.” They use it for claims review, contract analysis, customer support, coding, security triage, sales operations or internal search. A broad score can obscure the weakness that matters most. “A model is not ‘good’ or ‘bad,’” Kurtzig said. “It is good at some things and dangerous at others, and an aggregate score blends all of that into one number that hides exactly where it fails.” Public benchmark scores often come from tests such as GPQA, which uses difficult science questions, or SWE-bench, which evaluates software engineering tasks. Zhenwen Dai, CTO and co-founder of Trent AI, an AI security company, said companies should be careful about relying too heavily on scores from public tests. They can be useful signals, he said, but they can also encourage companies to overestimate how well a model will perform in their own environment. “A model may become better at the benchmark without becoming equally better at the real-world tasks a company actually needs to solve,” Dai told Newsweek. Vendor demos and public tests can miss the details that matter once a system enters a company’s environment. “Companies should evaluate AI at the level of the specific task or workflow, rather than relying on general model capability scores,” Dai said. What a buyer deploys may be far removed from the base model that performed well in a public test. The same underlying technology can behave differently once it is embedded inside a product, connected to tools or given permissions inside a company. Varun Badhwar, founder and CEO of Endor Labs, a software security company, sees the problem clearly in AI coding agents. His company runs the Agent Security League, a public benchmark for AI coding agents that extends research from Carnegie Mellon University. The benchmark tracks the gap between code that passes functional tests and code that is actually secure. “The benchmarks aren’t wrong—they’re measuring the wrong axis for an enterprise buyer,” Badhwar told Newsweek. “They measure capability: Can the model do the task? They’re largely silent on the properties that actually create enterprise liability—is the output safe, is it accountable, is it correct in a way you can defend later?” Badhwar cautioned against assuming a base model’s score carries cleanly into production. A company is using a full system, not an abstract model on a leaderboard. “You are not deploying the model,” he said. “You’re deploying the model, inside a harness, pointed at your data, under your constraints.” Human review also becomes more specific once AI is connected to tools, data and business processes. The point is not to have a person glance at every AI output. The question is where failure would be expensive, quiet or difficult to reverse. Patrick Sullivan, vice president of strategy and innovation at A-LIGN, a cybersecurity compliance company, said evaluations are most useful when companies can turn them into evidence for how an AI system performs in real work. “Benchmarks measure capability under clean conditions,” Sullivan told Newsweek. “Professional workflows are not clean.” Professional settings add unclear inputs, changing rules, internal systems and records that may need to be inspected later by customers, auditors or regulators. Once companies put AI systems into those settings, Sullivan said, they also need assurance: proof of how the system behaved, what controls were in place and whether a reviewer can reconstruct the decision later. “The right question isn’t ‘How well does this model perform?’” Sullivan said. “It’s ‘Can I produce evidence that it performed correctly, on my work, for the use case I deployed it against?’” Several executives described the same basic standard: Review should rise with risk. A tool that drafts an internal memo does not need the same oversight as one that affects a payment, security decision, health recommendation, legal right or compliance record. Badhwar said the review threshold should be tied to what the error could touch. “Anything touching money, security, regulated decisions, or anything that’s hard to reverse gets a human, regardless of how confident the model is or how high the aggregate benchmark sits,” he said. Expert review is also needed earlier, Dai said, when companies are deciding what to measure. A poorly designed evaluation can make a system look safer than it is. “The quality of the evaluation framework directly affects whether the deployment decision is valid,” Dai said. Clark pushed the concern into procurement. As capable, inexpensive models flood the market, he said, many buyers cannot answer basic questions about who built them, what they were trained on, how their behavior was shaped or where company data flows. “You wouldn’t onboard a supplier into your physical supply chain without knowing its origin,” Clark said. “The same diligence has to apply to your AI supply chain—especially in regulated and federal environments.” The concern has already moved beyond internal AI committees. This month, the U.S. government ordered Anthropic to block foreign nationals from accessing its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, citing national security concerns; Anthropic said it disagreed with the decision but disabled access to comply. Kurtzig said companies need to draw clearer boundaries around where AI can act on its own and where the consequences of a wrong answer are too high. “'Mostly right' is the wrong bar,” he said. “A single bad answer can outweigh a thousand good ones, so the real question is not how often the model is right. It is what happens when it is wrong.” Enterprise AI adoption is likely to keep moving quickly. The companies in the strongest position may not be the ones that simply pick the highest-scoring system. They will be the ones that can say where a tool works, where it needs review and where it should not act on its own. Clark framed testing as the thing that lets deployment move faster, rather than the thing that slows it down. “Speed is the payoff for testing the model against the job it’ll actually do, in the environment it’ll actually run, before you ship it—not after,” he said. ... data.title: ClearDent and Pearl are ‘Accelerating Access to Power of AI’ in Dental Field
data.ai_summary: Pearl, a Los Angeles-based dental AI solutions company, has partnered with ClearDent, a dental practice management platform founded in Burnaby, Canada in 2002, to integrate Pearl's Second Opinion chairside radiologic dental AI disease detection software with ClearDent's imaging toolset. The integration will allow Canadian dental practitioners to access AI-powered pathology detection for conditions including caries, calculus, and periapical radiolucency through ClearDent's Developer Program API. The partnership aims to expand access to AI-powered dental diagnostics across Canada, enabling dentists to deliver higher quality and more standardized patient care.
data.author: Knowlton Thomas
data.full_text:
Two companies innovating the dental field are collaborating.

Pearl, a dental AI solutions pioneer based out of Los Angeles, is partnering with ClearDent, which was founded in Burnaby in 2002 as a dental practice management platform that integrates scheduling, charting, treatment planning, billing, imaging, and patient engagement into a unified, secure system built specifically for Canadian regulatory and privacy standards.

The partnership will integrate Pearl’s Second Opinion chairside radiologic dental AI disease detection software with ClearDentʼs imaging toolset, according to a statement from the firms.

Second Opinion software delivers pathology detection for an array of conditions, including caries, calculus, and periapical radiolucency.

Through ClearDent’s Developer Program, Pearl’s API integration will allow practitioners a more powerful lens through which to view radiographs and develop diagnoses.

“Our partnership with Pearl is a proud addition to our growing partner ecosystem, and a logical step in our quest to further support Canadian dentists,” says Karl Schmidt, who served as Executive Vice President of Business Development at ClearDent.

“Through our work together, we’re helping those in the industry embrace the future of dentistry and incorporate the most innovative solutions in order to streamline and improve their practices,” he stated.

“Our partnership with ClearDent will markedly accelerate access to the power and benefits of AI for dental practices and clinicians throughout Canada,” commented Ophir Tanz, chief executive officer of Pearl.

“Second Opinion enables dentists to deliver higher quality and more standardized care for patients, and with ClearDent as a partner, more dental patients across Canada will see those benefits in their treatment outcomes,” said Tanz.

Pearl was founded in 2019.

data.full_text: LOS ANGELES & BURNABY, British Columbia--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Pearl, the global leader in dental AI solutions, and ClearDent, the leading dental software solution for Canadian dentists, today announced a partnership that will integrate Pearl's Second Opinion® chairside radiologic dental AI disease detection software with ClearDentʼs imaging toolset. As a member of ClearDent's Developer Program, Pearl will begin distributing Second Opinion® to ClearDent practices in Canada as an API-based integration available within ClearDent's practice management solution. The partnership will bring the full range of benefits of AI-assisted clinical care to a Canadian practitioner cohort that has established itself as among the most tech-forward in the world. "Our partnership with ClearDent will markedly accelerate access to the power and benefits of AI for dental practices and clinicians throughout Canada," said Ophir Tanz, CEO of Pearl. "Second Opinion® enables dentists to deliver higher quality and more standardized care for patients, and with ClearDent as a partner, more dental patients across Canada will see those benefits in their treatment outcomes." Pearl's Second Opinion® software delivers pathology detection for an array of conditions, including caries, calculus, and periapical radiolucency, among others. Through ClearDent's Developer Program, Pearl's API integration will allow practitioners to bring AI to bear seamlessly within their existing real-time clinical workflow providing a more powerful lens through which to view radiographs and develop diagnoses. "Our partnership with Pearl is a proud addition to our growing partner ecosystem, and a logical step in our quest to further support Canadian dentists," said Karl Schmidt, Executive Vice President of Business Development at ClearDent. "Through our work together, we're helping those in the industry embrace the future of dentistry and incorporate the most innovative solutions in order to streamline and improve their practices." With Second Opinion® recognized globally, having received clearance in Canada, the USA, Australia, New Zealand, and Europe, Pearl and ClearDent look forward to supporting Canadian dental professionals through joint educational initiatives, webinars, and events that advance the adoption of AI in everyday clinical practice. data.title: What is the Pearl that is being spammed? The entire process of cloud rental card arbitrage: as long as the rent is below 0.7U, it is profitable.
data.ai_summary: Pearl, a PoUW L1, allows GPU mining for AI inference, with a process to rent 4090/5090 cards under 0.7U/h and run a miner. Profit depends on daily PRL output and rental cost, with a formula for break-even. The article advises testing one card for 24 hours before scaling.

industries.name: Decentralized GPU/AI Compute Networks (training/inference, GPU renting, model hosting)

data.full_text:
Pearl 简介 ：基于 PoUW 的 L1，GPU 挖矿同时做 AI 推理；已主网上线，与 Together AI 合作，零预挖。 挖矿流程 ：租用 4090/5090（RunPod/VastAI，租金门槛 <0.7U/h）→ 生成钱包 → 配置矿机（pearlhash）→ SSH 运行。 收益关键 ：日净利润 = 日产 PRL × 币价 × 0.97 - 租金×24；币价波动与流动性是主要风险。 策略 ：优先低租金卡，先跑 24h 验证，勿盲目放大。

作者：TIGER

这两天圈子里被刷屏的 @prlnet 珍珠挖矿，本质是「去云算力平台租张 4090/5090，跑起来就出币」。Toni 老师的原话是 每日挖提卖的利润在 50% 以上，按当前币价 1.3–1.4U，只要你能租到 0.7U 以下的 4090 满血卡，就是赚的。

这篇把流程拆到傻瓜级，最后附一个自己能算账的收益模型，别只看话术，自己算清楚再上车。

一、Pearl 是什么（30 秒看懂）

PoUW（有用工作量证明）的 L1 公链：矿工的 GPU 不是在算无意义哈希，而是在做 AI 推理/训练里的矩阵乘法，挖矿和真实算力是同一份计算，额外开销仅约 10%。

2026 年 4 月主网上线， 已和 Together AI（NVIDIA 云合作伙伴）合作 ，用代币排放补贴 AI 推理成本（Gemma-4-31B-it-pearl 端点直接打 75 折）。

无预挖、无创始份额、无 VC，公平发射 —— 这是它叙事最硬的一点。

一句话：币价越涨，AI 推理越便宜，算力越多人挖 → 这是个会自我强化的飞轮。

二、开挖前准备

你只需要两样东西：

一个能租 4090/5090 的云算力账号

一个 Pearl 钱包地址

租卡平台（二选一，新手推荐 RunPod，界面友好）：

三、四步开挖（保姆级）

第 1 步｜租卡 进 RunPod/VastAI，筛选 RTX 4090 / 5090，认准「满血卡」（整卡、非分时切片）。 选卡铁律：租金 < 0.7 U/小时（按当前币价，这是盈亏分界线，下面第四节会算给你看）。

第 2 步｜生成 Pearl 钱包 打开 👉 http://compute.pearlresearch.ai/wallet 点生成，助记词务必离线抄好，复制你的钱包地址备用。

第 3 步｜配置矿机 打开 👉 https://pearlhash.xyz/#config 把上一步的钱包地址填进去，页面会生成一条一键启动命令/脚本，复制它。 （pearlhash 矿池费 3%，最低 1 PRL 起提，门槛很低。）

第 4 步｜SSH 进实例跑起来

在 RunPod/VastAI 里给实例配好 SSH 密钥并连接

把第 3 步复制的命令粘贴执行

看到算力上报、开始出币 → 收工，挂机即可

矿机本质是官方的 vLLM miner（CUDA），跑起来后 GPU 一边出 PRL 一边对外提供 AI 推理算力。

提币卖出：攒够 PRL 后可走 OTC（otc.lordofpearls.xyz / pearl-otc.com/marketplace）或跨链桥 pearlbridge.xyz 变现。

四、成本 / 收益测算（重点，自己算账别上头）

别只信「日利 50%+」，自己套公式：

核心公式

日净利润 = 单卡日产 PRL × 币价 × (1 − 3%矿池费) − 租金/小时 × 24

最简判断法（推荐） 只要满足：单卡每小时产出的 PRL 价值 > 每小时租金，你就在赚钱。 这正是 Toni 说的「租到 0.7U 以下就是赚」的来源 —— 当前币价下，一张 4090 每小时产出价值 ≈ 0.7U 出头。

盈亏平衡点（示例，数据请按 pearlhash 面板实时填）

假设租金 = 0.6 U/小时 → 日成本 = 0.6 × 24 = 14.4 U

假设币价 = 1.3 U

那么每天至少要产出：14.4 ÷ (1.3 × 0.97) ≈ 11.4 PRL/天 才回本

超过这个量，多挖的全是利润

两个杠杆

租金越低越好：盯紧 spot/竞价实例，0.4–0.5U 的 4090 利润空间最大

币价是双刃剑：涨了利润翻倍，跌破租金线立刻倒贴 —— 这就是为什么要每天看账，别无脑挂

五、风险提示（必须看完）

币价波动：测算全建立在 1.3U 上，币价腰斩你就从赚变亏，且早期代币波动极大。

卖出滑点：PRL 目前主要靠 OTC/桥变现，深度有限，大额卖出滑点和到账时间都要打折。

租卡是按秒烧钱：实例没跑满、配置出错、网络中断，矿不出来但租金照扣。

早期项目不确定性：主网刚上线、合作和叙事很性感，但同样意味着规则、产量、矿池都可能随时调整。

结论：这不是稳赚，是「在套利窗口存在期间、会算账的人能赚」。先租 1 张卡跑 24 小时，拿真实数据套上面的公式验证盈利，再决定要不要加杠杆放大。

工具直达：

DYOR，先小仓验证，算清楚再上车。🐚
